analysis.one_liner: Bans factories from discharging plastic pellets into U.S. waterways.
analysis.headline: The bill was never considered by the Senate committee it was assigned to and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the EPA to write a rule within 60 days prohibiting facilities that make, use, package, or transport plastic pellets from discharging those pellets into wastewater, stormwater, or any other waters of the United States. It also required the ban to be written into every relevant water discharge permit and performance standard. Plastic pellets are the raw material for nearly all plastic products, and spilled pellets wash into rivers and oceans.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use or live near rivers, lakes, and coastal waters, including fishing communities and local governments that bear cleanup costs, benefit from less pellet pollution in waterways.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to issue a final rule within 60 days prohibiting discharge of plastic pellets and other pre-production plastic from regulated facilities and from any point source that makes, uses, packages, or transports them.
Requires the prohibition to be reflected in all wastewater, stormwater, and other discharge permits issued under the Clean Water Act, as well as applicable performance standards.

Plastic pellets are small enough to escape containment, soak up pollutants, and be mistaken for food by fish, seabirds, and other wildlife; stopping discharges at the source prevents that contamination.

analysis.who_pays: Plastic polymer producers and plastics molding and packaging facilities, which would have to keep pellets out of their wastewater and runoff, potentially through containment equipment and process changes.

drawbacks.text: The bill ordered a final rule within 60 days of enactment, an unusually short deadline for a new EPA rule across many industrial categories, which could have produced rushed permitting conditions without full industry-specific analysis.

Facilities that make, use, package, or transport pellets would bear compliance costs; the bill did not fund assistance, so those costs could fall on smaller plastics processors and be passed to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit of keeping raw plastic pellets out of rivers and oceans is real and the compliance costs appear modest, since the requirement is essentially zero-discharge housekeeping at existing permitted facilities. The main design weakness was the extremely short 60-day rulemaking deadline rather than the substance of the ban.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Udall introduced the Plastic Pellet Free Waters Act on September 24, 2020, in the final weeks before the 2020 election.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote followed, and no senator cosponsored the bill.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and bills not passed by then expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastics manufacturers that discharge pellets avoided new federal discharge limits, since no rule was required before the bill expired.

for.name: Tom Udall
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico, bill's only sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Plastics manufacturing and packaging industry
against.role: Facilities that make, use, package, or transport plastic pellets
against.what_they_did: Would have been subject to the discharge prohibition; no support for the bill appeared in the record.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic senator introduced the bill with no cosponsors from either party, and no member of either party moved it forward.

industries.note: The bill would have prohibited these facilities from discharging plastic pellets into wastewater and stormwater, requiring containment and permit changes. Their interest in avoiding those requirements ran against cleaner waterways that ordinary people use.
